title: Richer isn't better
hookLine: "I'm richer than you, so I'm better" doesn't follow (Enchiridion 44)

cards: A twenty-year class reunion. Name tags, a slideshow, and a low hum of measuring. Who has the bigger house.
Who has the better job title. Who still looks thirty. Nobody says the next step out loud, but it hangs in the room: so they're doing better than me.
So I'm less than them. Epictetus heard the same hum in his own day, and in section forty-four he does something unexpected with it. He doesn't preach.

teach.b: Two arguments fail, he says. I'm richer than you, so I'm better than you. I'm more eloquent than you, so I'm better than you.
The conclusion doesn't come out of the premise. Two others work.
I'm richer than you, so my property is greater than yours. I'm more eloquent than you, so my speech is better than yours. Those compare like with like: money with money, speaking with speaking.

teach.h: YOU ARE NEITHER PROPERTY NOR SPEECH.
teach.b: Then the hinge, one short sentence: but you are neither property nor speech. The comparison is real, but it compares things you have, or things you do.
The jump from my things are bigger to I am better quietly assumes that you are your things. A Stoic says you're not. You're the one who uses them, who judges, who chooses.

teach.h: IT FREES THE WINNER AND THE LOSER.
teach.b: And this frees both sides. It takes the air out of the reunion bragging. It also takes the sting out of losing the comparison.
Their house is bigger. Fine: that says something true about two houses, and nothing at all about two people.

You can admire someone's skill, or envy their savings, and still notice that it doesn't follow. The same check works on the voice that says I'm worse at this, so I'm worth less. That doesn't follow either.

how: People practicing Stoicism sometimes catch comparisons that jump from 'they have more' to 'they are better' and correct the logic, as in Enchiridion 44.

o: richer food isn't always the better meal
a pricier choice isn't always the better buy
more money means more property, not a better person

s: Epictetus says being rich is bad
he says richer means more property, which is fine. it just doesn't make you better.
section forty-four is built as a logic check
two arguments that fail, two that work, and the reason why.

games.q: at the reunion, an old classmate says: I make twice what you do, so I've done better than you. what does Epictetus say?
o: doesn't follow. twice the salary, yes; a better person, no.
find something you're better at, and say so.
games.why: twice the money means twice the money. you are neither property nor speech, so the step to 'better' doesn't follow.

practice: Bring to mind one comparison that's been running in your head lately, a salary, a body, a family, a follower count, and say the full sentence with its hidden last step: they have more, so they're better than me.
Then break it the way Epictetus does: their things are more, true; so they are better? Doesn't follow, and you can rest there a moment.

wordCard.voice: Richer isn't better. Epictetus checks the logic: more money means more property, not a better person. You are neither property nor speech. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: doesn't follow. More property, more polish, and still not a better person. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.
